answer: Implemented stable_unique in sequences.py. It iterates the input once (works with any iterable, including generators), appending the first occurrence of each equality-distinct value to a result list, preserving input order. Hashable items are tracked in a set for O(1) average lookups; items whose hash() raises TypeError (e.g., lists, dicts) are tracked in a separate list and compared with `==` via any(), so unhashable values are supported. Input values are never mutated—only references are stored. Public API (function name, signature, docstring) and the unrelated reversed_copy function are unchanged. Manual reasoning checks: [1,2,1,3] -> [1,2,3]; generator input consumed lazily once; [[1],[2],[1]] -> [[1],[2]]; [{'a':1},{'a':1}] -> [{'a':1}]; mixed hashable/unhashable inputs work. Note: float('nan') values are never equal to themselves, so each NaN is kept (consistent with equality semantics); values that are equal across the hashable/unhashable boundary (unusual custom types) could be duplicated—a bounded check, not a formal proof. Source reference: sequences.py, stable_unique function (lines 4-21 after edit).
